fixes.explanation: That's it, friend. Saul, king of Israel, kept David with him from that day, and the text says he did not let David return to his father's house. David had been going back and forth between Saul and his dad's sheep (1 Samuel 17:15). Now that back and forth is over.

Yes! Jonathan, Saul's son, gave David his robe, then his tunic, his sword, his bow and his belt. That's a king's son handing over his own gear. I'd have a hard time handing over my chef's hat, so this is a whole other level.
Right. The text says David's rise was pleasing in the sight of all the people, and of Saul's officers as well. Everybody was on board, officers included. Hold onto that, because the story isn't over.
Not quite. The text says Saul was furious and resented the song. He said, “They have ascribed tens of thousands to David, but only thousands to me.” No sing-along there.
That would've been a sweet ending, but it isn't what the text says. Saul was furious and resented the song. Then he asked, “What more can he have but the kingdom?” That's not pride.
That's the word. From that day forward, Saul kept a jealous eye on David. The song was over, but that jealous eye stayed on him.
I wish it had gone that way. But the text says Saul hurled the spear, thinking, “I will pin David to the wall.” I think this part is heavy. Nobody was handed anything.
Not this time, friend. Saul hurled the spear, thinking, “I will pin David to the wall.” But the text says David eluded him twice. So no pinning happened.
Right. Saul hurled the spear, thinking, “I will pin David to the wall.” But David eluded him twice. The pinning didn't happen.
Yes. David continued to prosper in all his ways, because the LORD was with him. Send him out with a thousand men, and he still thrives. Meanwhile, I get one timer to watch and I still burn a batch.
No wandering for this guy. The text says he led the troops out to battle and back, and he continued to prosper in all his ways. The reason given is that the LORD was with him.

The Philistines do come up in this passage, but David doesn't ask for that here. His answer is, “Who am I, and what is my family or my father’s clan in Israel, that I should become the son-in-law of the king?” I think he's wondering if he's even the right guy. He's asking about himself, not making a request.
Yes. David replied, “Does it seem trivial in your sight to be the son-in-law of the king? I am a poor man and lightly esteemed.” He doesn't puff himself up, and I honestly respect that.

Yes. When the servants reported the terms to David, he was pleased to become the king's son-in-law. Saul intended David's death at the hands of the Philistines. But what the text tells us about David is that he was pleased.
Here's what the text says. When the servants reported these terms to David, he was pleased to become the king's son-in-law. So pleased is the word, not displeased. That's the reaction the text gives.
Yes, two hundred. David and his men killed two hundred Philistines before the wedding day arrived. Saul asked for a hundred, so David brought back double. He presented them as payment in full.
That's the word. When Saul realized the LORD was with David and that Michal loved David, he grew even more afraid of David. The fear was already there (1 Samuel 18:12), and the text says it grew.
Not at all, friend. The text says, “So from then on Saul was David’s enemy.” That comes right after Saul gave Michal to David in marriage. So peace isn't what the text shows.

I can see why you'd wonder, with Saul so afraid of him. But the text says David's name was highly esteemed. That means respected, not criticized. Every time the Philistine commanders came out for battle, David was more successful than all of Saul's officers.

I spent years forgotten in the back of a junk drawer, and this isn't that. The text says David was more successful than all of Saul's officers, so his name was highly esteemed. Forgotten isn't the word.
